screens.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Calculations and Estimation
screens.narratorSegment: In system design interviews, careful measurement starts with quick, practical math. You will learn how to convert user counts and usage patterns into rough QPS numbers, storage volumes, and bandwidth needs that shape major architectural decisions. These back-of-the-envelope calculations are not about exact digits; they are about order of magnitude — do we need megabytes or petabytes, hundreds or hundreds of thousands of requests per second? We’ll use concrete examples like a photo-sharing service to show how user assumptions turn into QPS, daily storage, and peak bandwidth. I’ll also give you a shortlist of power-of-two memory numbers and a set of latency landmarks to reason about caching and cross-datacenter tradeoffs. Finally, we’ll highlight frequent mistakes — like forgetting peak traffic or mixing bits and bytes — and simple strategies to avoid them. By the end of this lesson you’ll be able to produce quick, defensible estimates and explain how those numbers influence choices such as object storage, CDN use, and caching layers. Consider this the practical lens you use before committing to a design.

keyIdea.title: Why quick estimates matter
keyIdea.text: Order-of-magnitude calculations reveal scale early so you can choose appropriate storage, caching, and network strategies.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Overview
Back-of-the-Envelope Calculations
Turn user and behavior assumptions into quick QPS, storage, and bandwidth estimates to guide design decisions.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

In this chapter you will practice common estimation patterns, memorize a few handy numeric landmarks, and learn the common mistakes that make interview math look shaky. The goal is defensible, fast reasoning rather than precise accounting.

Coming up: QPS from users, storage sizing, bandwidth & latency rules of thumb.

Concept Map
QPS & Peak
Estimate requests per second from DAU and activity.
Storage
Multiply items by size and retention to get TB/PB scale.
Bandwidth & CDN
Use peak QPS * payload to reason about CDN vs origin load.
Explore Key Topics
QPS
From users to requests per second — the core driver of capacity planning.
Storage
Item size × count × retention quickly reveals TB vs PB needs.
Bandwidth
Peak load times payload size tells you if you need a CDN or more origin capacity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter teaches four practical skills you will use in every system design problem. First, you will understand why quantitative estimation matters: it exposes whether a service needs object stores, sharding, or heavy caching before you draw architecture diagrams. Second, you will learn how to compute basic QPS from user counts and behavior; that allows you to size ingress, A P I servers, and load balancers. Third, you will practice storage estimation: multiplying per-item size by count and retention time to decide between relational stores, object storage, or distributed file systems. Fourth, you will memorize and apply common numeric landmarks — powers of two for quick unit conversion and a set of latency numbers — so you can reason about caching and cross-datacenter tradeoffs. Each skill reduces uncertainty and helps you explain trade-offs clearly under time pressure. You’ll practice with concrete examples and leave with simple checklists to avoid the most common interview mistakes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Alongside the core skills, you must internalize common pitfalls and a short practice routine. First, always state units and be consistent with bits versus bytes and powers-of-two versus powers-of-ten — unit confusion is a frequent error. Second, practice breaking large calculations into steps: compute daily totals first, then convert to rates and apply peak windows. Third, rehearse a small checklist each time: estimate DAU, actions per DAU, average payload size, retention, and expected peak concentration. Fourth, use latency landmarks to choose caching and data placement; for example, in-memory access is orders of magnitude faster than SSD or cross-continent calls, which justifies adding a cache for hot user objects. These practice habits reduce arithmetic mistakes and ensure your interviewer sees clear reasoning, not guesswork. You will practice these routines with a messaging app activity and an assessment walkthrough in later slides.

keyIdea.title: Practice routine
keyIdea.text: Use a short checklist and consistent units to avoid arithmetic and unit mistakes under interview pressure.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.5 › Practice & Pitfalls
Checklist for every estimate
  • State units clearly (KB, MB, GB, QPS, ms).
  • Compute daily totals before rates.
  • Apply a peak multiplier and a peak window.
  • Round to powers of two or ten for order-of-magnitude.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
Common mistake & fix
Mixing bits and bytes or forgetting peak traffic leads to wrong capacity choices. Fix by writing unit conversions explicitly and computing both average and peak QPS in your sketch.
Mnemonic visual: write DAU → actions → daily total → seconds/day → QPS → peak multiplier.
Use latency landmarks
When you cite latency numbers, explain the impact. For example, if cross-datacenter is ~150 ms, you cannot use it for tight synchronous operations; cache or local store is preferable.
Explain your rounding
State whether you round to powers of two or ten. Interviewers value the trade-off reasoning more than precise digits.

screens.title: What is a back-of-the-envelope calculation?
screens.narratorSegment: A back-of-the-envelope calculation is a quick, approximate estimate aimed at determining order of magnitude rather than exact values. In systems design contexts you use it to decide whether a problem requires a single server, horizontal sharding, object storage, or global CDNs. The defining feature is simple arithmetic applied to clearly stated assumptions: user counts, actions per user, average payload size, and retention. For example, if you know daily active users and uploads per user, you can multiply to get a daily count and then convert that to QPS by dividing by the number of seconds per day. Importantly, these estimates should include both average and peak calculations. A common misconception is that precise numbers matter; they do not for architectural direction — orders of magnitude do. Another pitfall is failing to state units; always call out bytes versus bits and seconds versus milliseconds. A concrete example: given 100 million daily uploads of 1 MB each, you quickly see hundreds of TB per day and realize single-node storage is impossible. Key takeaway: use simple steps, state assumptions, and convert to rate and scale so your architectural choices are grounded in numbers.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Fast, assumption-driven math for order-of-magnitude insights that guide design choices.

content.html:
Core Concept Definition
Back-of-the-envelope calculation
Quick estimates to reveal scale and justify architecture
Steps to perform an estimate
  1. State user counts and conversion to DAU (if given).
  2. Estimate actions per user per day (uploads, views, messages).
  3. Multiply to get daily totals, then convert to QPS by dividing by 86,400 seconds.
  4. Apply a peak multiplier using a peak window to get peak QPS.
Concrete example
If 100M DAU upload 1 photo each per day: daily uploads = 100M. Average QPS = 100M / 86,400 ≈ 1,157. If 20% of traffic is in 4 peak hours, peak QPS ≈ 1,388. That order shows you need horizontally scalable upload servers and asynchronous storage.
Why this matters
  • Determines whether to use object storage or a relational DB.
  • Guides caching and CDN decisions by revealing bandwidth needs.
  • Helps avoid under-provisioning and over-engineering early in design.
Key Takeaway

A few clear assumptions and simple arithmetic tell you the scale and the right class of infrastructure to consider.

screens.title: From DAU to QPS: a step-by-step recipe
screens.narratorSegment: Converting user behavior into QPS is a repeatable process you should rehearse. Start with the total number of users and convert to daily active users, because DAU drives day-to-day traffic. Next, estimate actions per DAU per day for the specific operation you care about — uploads, message sends, or views. Multiply DAU by actions per day to get daily requests. To reach average QPS, divide the daily requests by the number of seconds in a day, 86,400. To estimate peak QPS, identify your peak window and what fraction of traffic happens during that window. For example, if 20% of daily uploads occur during a 4-hour peak, scale the average QPS by 24/4 and multiply by 0.20. A common misconception is to multiply by 0.20 without accounting for the shorter window; always expand the per-second rate to the peak window size before applying the traffic fraction. Concrete example: with 1 billion total users, 10% DAU equals 100M DAU, one upload each gives 100M daily uploads, average QPS ≈ 1,157, and peak QPS using the 4-hour 20% model becomes ≈ 1,388. That figure determines how many parallel upload servers and front-end load capacity you need.

keyIdea.title: Recipe
keyIdea.text: DAU × actions/day → daily total → divide by 86,400 → apply peak window and fraction for peak QPS.

content.html:
Process Flow
From DAU to QPS
A reproducible sequence for average and peak rates
1
Estimate DAU
Convert total users to Daily Active Users using an interview assumption. State the percentage you use and why.
2
Multiply actions per DAU
Actions per DAU per day gives you daily request volume for the feature in question.
3
Convert to QPS
Divide daily requests by 86,400 seconds to get average QPS, then compute peak QPS using window scaling and fraction of traffic.
Worked Example — photo upload
Assume 1B users, 10% DAU = 100M. One upload per DAU → 100M uploads/day. Average QPS = 100M / 86,400 ≈ 1,157. If 20% of uploads happen in a 4-hour peak window, peak QPS = average × (24/4) × 0.20 ≈ 1,388. That peak number is the operational target for the upload path.
Common Mistake

Applying the traffic fraction without scaling for the shorter window underestimates peak QPS. Always expand to the short window first, then apply the fraction.

screens.title: Storage estimation: from item size to multi-year totals
screens.narratorSegment: Storage estimation is straightforward but its implications are dramatic. Start with average item size and daily item count. Multiply to get daily storage growth, then multiply by 365 and by the retention window in years to estimate long-term storage. For example, if a photo service produces 100 million photos per day and each photo is 1 MB, daily storage is 100 TB. Over ten years that becomes about 365 PB — which immediately tells you object storage and distributed file systems are required rather than a single relational database. Be careful with units and powers: say MB, TB, or PB explicitly. A common misconception is to treat 1,000 MB as 1 GB; decide whether you use powers of 1000 or 1024 and state it. Another pitfall is forgetting metadata, thumbnails, or multiple sizes; include per-object overhead in your per-item estimate when warranted. Use rounding to the nearest power of two or ten to keep the estimate communicable. The practical outcome of these calculations is a constraint: when storage reaches hundreds of TB or PB you must plan architecture for durability, replication, lifecycle policies, and cost-effective cold storage.

keyIdea.title: Storage formula
keyIdea.text: Daily storage = item size × daily count. Long-term = daily × 365 × years. Round to powers for clarity.

content.html:
Process Flow
Storage Estimation
Item size × daily count → daily TB → multi-year PB
Step-by-step
  1. Pick average item size (include thumbnails/metadata).
  2. Multiply by daily item count to get bytes/day.
  3. Convert to TB/day, then multiply by 365 × retention years.
  4. Round to nearest power of ten or two and state assumptions.
Example
100M photos/day × 1 MB/photo = 100,000,000 MB = 100 TB/day. Over 10 years: 100 TB/day × 365 × 10 ≈ 365 PB. This scale indicates object storage and lifecycle policies.
Implications
  • Hundreds of TB or PB justify object storage and distributed systems.
  • Consider replication, cold storage, and deletion policies to control cost.
  • Metadata and derived assets (thumbnails) can multiply storage — include them in estimates.
Key Takeaway

Long-term retention turns modest daily growth into PB-scale storage; plan storage class and lifecycle from the estimate.

screens.title: Bandwidth estimation and the role of CDNs
screens.narratorSegment: Bandwidth estimation ties QPS and payload together to reveal egress and origin load. Start with peak QPS for the operation you’re analyzing, then multiply by average payload size to get bytes per second. Convert that into GB/s or Gbps to compare against network capacity. For example, if peak photo views are about 13,888 QPS and each photo is 1 MB, peak download bandwidth is roughly 13.8 GB/s. That number often exceeds what origin servers should handle, indicating a need for a CDN to serve cached content closer to users and offload egress from the origin. A common misconception is to look only at average bandwidth; CDNs are used to meet the bursty nature of peak windows and to reduce latency for users. Also be explicit about bits versus bytes when converting to Gbps. In interviews, explain how a CDN reduces origin capacity, lowers latency for geographically distributed users, and can dramatically change cost and provisioning decisions. Use the peak bandwidth number as the starting point when choosing caching and distribution strategies. Bandwidth estimation and the role of CDNs means peak bandwidth = peak qps × payload size. use it to decide cdn use and origin capacity.. In practical terms, use peak qps and payload size to reason about egress and cdn needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bandwidth formula
keyIdea.text: Peak bandwidth = peak QPS × payload size. Use it to decide CDN use and origin capacity.

content.html:
Core Concept
Bandwidth & CDN
Peak QPS × payload → bytes/sec → Gbps
Worked bandwidth example
If peak QPS for photo views ≈ 13,888 and each photo ≈ 1 MB, peak download bandwidth ≈ 13,888 MB/s ≈ 13.8 GB/s. This magnitude typically justifies CDN offload and edge caching to reduce origin egress and improve latency.
Conversion tip
When converting to Gbps, multiply GB/s by 8 to get Gbit/s and be explicit about using 1000 or 1024 bases. State your choice in the interview.
Why CDNs help
  • Serve cached objects near users to reduce origin bandwidth and latency.
  • Absorb traffic spikes and reduce the number of origin servers required.
  • Allow origin to focus on dynamic or authenticated content while edge handles static assets.
Key Takeaway

Peak bandwidth often dictates CDN use; express bandwidth in Gbps and justify edge caching from the peak number.

screens.title: Key numbers to memorize: powers of two and latency landmarks
screens.narratorSegment: A small vocabulary of numeric landmarks speeds estimation and helps you reason about trade-offs. For storage and memory, memorize common powers of two: two to the ten is about one thousand (KB), two to the twenty is roughly one million (MB), two to the thirty is about one billion (GB), and two to the forty is about one trillion (TB). These let you convert quickly between units. Equally important are latency landmarks for performance reasoning: L1 cache is sub-nanosecond, main memory references are around 100 ns, reading 4K randomly from an SSD is roughly 150 microseconds, disk seek times are on the order of 10 ms, and a cross-continent round trip is about 150 ms. Knowing these magnitudes helps you justify where to place data — in-memory caches versus remote storage — and explains why a cache can reduce latency by orders of magnitude. A common misconception is treating these as precise measurements; they are approximations meant to compare alternatives. In interviews, cite the landmark and explain how it changes your design: for example, fetching small user profile data from memory (100 ns) is vastly faster than a remote SSD or cross-region call.

keyIdea.text: Powers of two for unit conversions and latency landmarks for placement decisions (cache vs remote storage).

content.html:
Reference
Powers of Two & Latency Landmarks
Quick unit conversions and timing anchors for design decisions
Powers of two (approx)
  • 2^10 ≈ 1 thousand (KB)
  • 2^20 ≈ 1 million (MB)
  • 2^30 ≈ 1 billion (GB)
  • 2^40 ≈ 1 trillion (TB)
Use these to round quickly and keep orders of magnitude clear.
Latency landmarks (approx)
  • L1 cache reference: 0.5 ns
  • Main memory reference: ~100 ns
  • Read 4K from SSD: ~150 µs
  • Disk seek: ~10 ms
  • Cross-continent round trip: ~150 ms
These magnitudes explain why in-memory caches reduce latency dramatically compared to remote storage.

screens.title: Latency implications: choose where to put data
screens.narratorSegment: Latency numbers are not trivia — they directly influence where you store and how you fetch data. Compare four common options: in-memory cache on the same server, local SSD, local HDD, and a remote datacenter. In-memory reads are around 100 ns and are ideal for frequently accessed user objects like profiles or session state. SSD reads are on the order of 150 microseconds for small random reads; they are acceptable for moderately hot data but still two to three orders of magnitude slower than memory. HDD seeks are measured in milliseconds and are unsuitable for low-latency interactive reads. Remote datacenter calls include network round-trip times that can be hundreds of milliseconds, making them impractical for synchronous user-visible operations. A concrete example: if a user profile is frequently read, serving it from an in-memory cache gives sub-millisecond responses and reduces end-to-end latency significantly versus fetching from a remote SSD. A common misconception is assuming all persistent stores are equally suitable for reads; always match access patterns and latency requirements. Key takeaway: use memory for hot reads, SSD for warm data, disk for cold storage, and avoid cross-region syncs for latency-sensitive paths.

content.html:
Comparison
Latency & Storage Options
Options & typical latency
In-memory (RAM)~100 ns
SSD (4K random)~150 µs
HDD seek~10 ms
Cross-continent~150 ms
Use these anchors to argue for caches and locality during interviews.
Concrete design consequence
If user profile reads are frequent, an in-memory cache reduces latency and database load by orders of magnitude. If writes are less frequent, consider cache invalidation or write-through strategies. Avoid designs that require cross-region syncs for every interactive operation.
Common Mistake

Choosing storage solely on durability without considering access latency leads to poor user experience. State access patterns first.

screens.title: Common estimation mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Interview estimations can go wrong in predictable ways. The first and biggest mistake is skipping calculations entirely; never design without at least rough numbers. The second is being overly precise: avoid implying unwarranted precision — round to the nearest power of two or ten and justify it. Third, mixing units and failing to state whether you’re using powers-of-ten or powers-of-two leads to confusion; explicitly state units and conversion basis. Fourth, arithmetic errors are common under pressure; break calculations into smaller steps and call out intermediate values to let the interviewer follow your logic. Fifth, ignoring peak load and only quoting average QPS underprovisions systems; always compute peak with a reasonable window and fraction. Practical strategies: use a short checklist, write intermediate results, round early and state your rounding, and double-check units. A quick mental habit is to compute daily totals first, then rates, then peak. These safeguards make your estimates defensible and show the interviewer that your choices are grounded in numbers rather than guesswork. Common Mistake
Estimation Pitfalls & Fixes
Frequent mistakes
  • Skipping the calculation entirely.
  • Overstating precision instead of rounding.
  • Mixing bits and bytes or 1000 vs 1024 without saying so.
  • Using averages without computing peaks.
Practical fixes
  1. Write unit conversions explicitly.
  2. Show intermediate numbers so errors are visible and fixable.
  3. Round to powers of two or ten and state the rounding.
  4. Always compute peak QPS using a peak window and fraction.
These techniques make your reasoning transparent and let the interviewer focus on trade-offs.

screens.title: Activity: Estimate a messaging app (step-by-step)
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s work a concrete estimation exercise for a messaging app. Assume 2 billion total users and 50% daily active rate. That gives 1 billion DAU. If each DAU sends 20 text messages per day, total daily messages = 20 billion. To find average QPS for sending messages, divide 20 billion by 86,400 seconds, which yields about 231,481 QPS on average. Interviews often require peak estimates: if peak is 3× average concentrated in a 4-hour window, first compute average per-second inside that window by scaling with 24/4 then multiply by the peak fraction or factor; the result will be an order-of-magnitude higher and suggests the send path must support hundreds of thousands of requests per second. For storage, assume each message is 1 KB including metadata. Daily storage is 20 billion KB ≈ 20 TB per day (20 billion KB ÷ 1,000,000 KB/GB ≈ 20,000 GB = 20 TB). Over five years, that becomes roughly 36.5 PB. A common misconception is to forget metadata or to use inconsistent unit bases; always state your assumptions. This guided calculation shows how the same checklist produces QPS, peak, and long-term storage numbers you can use to choose storage tiers and sharding strategies.

Hands-on Activity
Messaging App Estimation
Step-by-step arithmetic you can show on a whiteboard
Assumptions
  • Total users: 2,000,000,000
  • DAU: 50% → 1,000,000,000
  • Messages per DAU per day: 20
  • Avg message size (with metadata): 1 KB
Calculated results
Daily messages = 1,000,000,000 × 20 = 20,000,000,000. Average QPS = 20,000,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 231,481 QPS. If peak = 3× average concentrated over 4 hours, expect peak QPS in the hundreds of thousands. Daily storage = 20B messages × 1 KB ≈ 20 TB/day. Over 5 years ≈ 20 TB/day × 365 × 5 ≈ 36.5 PB.
Why this matters
Hundreds of thousands of QPS on the sending path implies you need horizontally scalable ingestion, partitioned queues, and shards. Multi-petabyte storage requires object storage with lifecycle policies. Always state assumptions and add safety margins for growth.
Check Your Understanding

Try re-running the numbers if messages average 2 KB instead of 1 KB and note how storage doubles while QPS stays the same.

screens.title: Assessment example: video streaming capacity calculation
screens.narratorSegment: We’ll walk a consistent calculation for the assessment question about a video streaming service. Start by computing total viewing hours per day: 500 million DAU × 2 hours/user = 1,000,000,000 hours. Convert hours into seconds by multiplying by 3,600 to get total seconds of viewing. Multiply by the bitrate to get total bits transferred per day. Using 1 Mbps per stream as the bitrate, total daily bits = 1,000,000,000 hours × 3,600 sec/hour × 1,000,000 bits/sec = 3.6 × 10^15 bits. Convert to bytes by dividing by 8, then to petabytes using 10^15 bytes per PB (or state your 1000-based choice). Doing that yields roughly 450 PB per day with the 1000-base conversion used in the example. Average bandwidth is total bits per day divided by 86,400 seconds, which gives on the order of 4.16 × 10^13 bits/sec or about 41,600 Gbps, assuming 1000-based unit conversion. A common source of confusion is mixing 1000 and 1024 bases or bits and bytes; explicitly state conversions and pick one basis. In an interview, explain each step and state rounding choices. The key is consistent units and showing how the magnitude leads to infrastructure implications like CDN egress, peering, and capacity planning.

Assessment Walkthrough
Video streaming capacity example
Structured calculation (show on whiteboard)
// Given
DAU = 500,000,000
hours_per_user = 2
bitrate = 1 Mbps

// Total viewing hours per day
total_hours = DAU * hours_per_user = 1,000,000,000 hours

// Convert to seconds and bits
total_bits = total_hours * 3600 * 1,000,000 = 3.6e15 bits

// Convert to bytes and then to PB (1000-based)
bytes = total_bits / 8 = 4.5e14 bytes
petabytes = bytes / (1000**5) ≈ 450 PB

// Average bandwidth (bits/sec)
avg_bps = total_bits / 86400 ≈ 4.16e13 bps ≈ 41,600 Gbps
Note: state whether you use 1000 or 1024 base and keep units consistent throughout.
Interpretation
A multi-hundred-petabyte daily egress and tens of thousands of Gbps average bandwidth indicate global CDN egress, peering contracts, and large origin capacity. Mention cost and operational implications briefly to show trade-off awareness.
Misconception

Inconsistent unit conversions cause wildly different answers. Publish conversions explicitly and round deliberately.

fullNarratorScript:
In system design interviews, careful measurement starts with quick, practical math. You will learn how to convert user counts and usage patterns into rough QPS numbers, storage volumes, and bandwidth needs that shape major architectural decisions. These back-of-the-envelope calculations are not about exact digits; they are about order of magnitude — do we need megabytes or petabytes, hundreds or hundreds of thousands of requests per second? We’ll use concrete examples like a photo-sharing service to show how user assumptions turn into QPS, daily storage, and peak bandwidth. I’ll also give you a shortlist of power-of-two memory numbers and a set of latency landmarks to reason about caching and cross-datacenter tradeoffs. Finally, we’ll highlight frequent mistakes — like forgetting peak traffic or mixing bits and bytes — and simple strategies to avoid them. By the end of this lesson you’ll be able to produce quick, defensible estimates and explain how those numbers influence choices such as object storage, CDN use, and caching layers. Consider this the practical lens you use before committing to a design.

This chapter teaches four practical skills you will use in every system design problem. First, you will understand why quantitative estimation matters: it exposes whether a service needs object stores, sharding, or heavy caching before you draw architecture diagrams. Second, you will learn how to compute basic QPS from user counts and behavior; that allows you to size ingress, A P I servers, and load balancers. Third, you will practice storage estimation: multiplying per-item size by count and retention time to decide between relational stores, object storage, or distributed file systems. Fourth, you will memorize and apply common numeric landmarks — powers of two for quick unit conversion and a set of latency numbers — so you can reason about caching and cross-datacenter tradeoffs. Each skill reduces uncertainty and helps you explain trade-offs clearly under time pressure. You’ll practice with concrete examples and leave with simple checklists to avoid the most common interview mistakes.

Alongside the core skills, you must internalize common pitfalls and a short practice routine. First, always state units and be consistent with bits versus bytes and powers-of-two versus powers-of-ten — unit confusion is a frequent error. Second, practice breaking large calculations into steps: compute daily totals first, then convert to rates and apply peak windows. Third, rehearse a small checklist each time: estimate DAU, actions per DAU, average payload size, retention, and expected peak concentration. Fourth, use latency landmarks to choose caching and data placement; for example, in-memory access is orders of magnitude faster than SSD or cross-continent calls, which justifies adding a cache for hot user objects. These practice habits reduce arithmetic mistakes and ensure your interviewer sees clear reasoning, not guesswork. You will practice these routines with a messaging app activity and an assessment walkthrough in later slides.

A back-of-the-envelope calculation is a quick, approximate estimate aimed at determining order of magnitude rather than exact values. In systems design contexts you use it to decide whether a problem requires a single server, horizontal sharding, object storage, or global CDNs. The defining feature is simple arithmetic applied to clearly stated assumptions: user counts, actions per user, average payload size, and retention. For example, if you know daily active users and uploads per user, you can multiply to get a daily count and then convert that to QPS by dividing by the number of seconds per day. Importantly, these estimates should include both average and peak calculations. A common misconception is that precise numbers matter; they do not for architectural direction — orders of magnitude do. Another pitfall is failing to state units; always call out bytes versus bits and seconds versus milliseconds. A concrete example: given 100 million daily uploads of 1 MB each, you quickly see hundreds of TB per day and realize single-node storage is impossible. Key takeaway: use simple steps, state assumptions, and convert to rate and scale so your architectural choices are grounded in numbers.

Converting user behavior into QPS is a repeatable process you should rehearse. Start with the total number of users and convert to daily active users, because DAU drives day-to-day traffic. Next, estimate actions per DAU per day for the specific operation you care about — uploads, message sends, or views. Multiply DAU by actions per day to get daily requests. To reach average QPS, divide the daily requests by the number of seconds in a day, 86,400. To estimate peak QPS, identify your peak window and what fraction of traffic happens during that window. For example, if 20% of daily uploads occur during a 4-hour peak, scale the average QPS by 24/4 and multiply by 0.20. A common misconception is to multiply by 0.20 without accounting for the shorter window; always expand the per-second rate to the peak window size before applying the traffic fraction. Concrete example: with 1 billion total users, 10% DAU equals 100M DAU, one upload each gives 100M daily uploads, average QPS ≈ 1,157, and peak QPS using the 4-hour 20% model becomes ≈ 1,388. That figure determines how many parallel upload servers and front-end load capacity you need.

Storage estimation is straightforward but its implications are dramatic. Start with average item size and daily item count. Multiply to get daily storage growth, then multiply by 365 and by the retention window in years to estimate long-term storage. For example, if a photo service produces 100 million photos per day and each photo is 1 MB, daily storage is 100 TB. Over ten years that becomes about 365 PB — which immediately tells you object storage and distributed file systems are required rather than a single relational database. Be careful with units and powers: say MB, TB, or PB explicitly. A common misconception is to treat 1,000 MB as 1 GB; decide whether you use powers of 1000 or 1024 and state it. Another pitfall is forgetting metadata, thumbnails, or multiple sizes; include per-object overhead in your per-item estimate when warranted. Use rounding to the nearest power of two or ten to keep the estimate communicable. The practical outcome of these calculations is a constraint: when storage reaches hundreds of TB or PB you must plan architecture for durability, replication, lifecycle policies, and cost-effective cold storage.

Bandwidth estimation ties QPS and payload together to reveal egress and origin load. Start with peak QPS for the operation you’re analyzing, then multiply by average payload size to get bytes per second. Convert that into GB/s or Gbps to compare against network capacity. For example, if peak photo views are about 13,888 QPS and each photo is 1 MB, peak download bandwidth is roughly 13.8 GB/s. That number often exceeds what origin servers should handle, indicating a need for a CDN to serve cached content closer to users and offload egress from the origin. A common misconception is to look only at average bandwidth; CDNs are used to meet the bursty nature of peak windows and to reduce latency for users. Also be explicit about bits versus bytes when converting to Gbps. In interviews, explain how a CDN reduces origin capacity, lowers latency for geographically distributed users, and can dramatically change cost and provisioning decisions. Use the peak bandwidth number as the starting point when choosing caching and distribution strategies. Bandwidth estimation and the role of CDNs means peak bandwidth = peak qps × payload size. use it to decide cdn use and origin capacity.. In practical terms, use peak qps and payload size to reason about egress and cdn needs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A small vocabulary of numeric landmarks speeds estimation and helps you reason about trade-offs. For storage and memory, memorize common powers of two: two to the ten is about one thousand (KB), two to the twenty is roughly one million (MB), two to the thirty is about one billion (GB), and two to the forty is about one trillion (TB). These let you convert quickly between units. Equally important are latency landmarks for performance reasoning: L1 cache is sub-nanosecond, main memory references are around 100 ns, reading 4K randomly from an SSD is roughly 150 microseconds, disk seek times are on the order of 10 ms, and a cross-continent round trip is about 150 ms. Knowing these magnitudes helps you justify where to place data — in-memory caches versus remote storage — and explains why a cache can reduce latency by orders of magnitude. A common misconception is treating these as precise measurements; they are approximations meant to compare alternatives. In interviews, cite the landmark and explain how it changes your design: for example, fetching small user profile data from memory (100 ns) is vastly faster than a remote SSD or cross-region call.

Latency numbers are not trivia — they directly influence where you store and how you fetch data. Compare four common options: in-memory cache on the same server, local SSD, local HDD, and a remote datacenter. In-memory reads are around 100 ns and are ideal for frequently accessed user objects like profiles or session state. SSD reads are on the order of 150 microseconds for small random reads; they are acceptable for moderately hot data but still two to three orders of magnitude slower than memory. HDD seeks are measured in milliseconds and are unsuitable for low-latency interactive reads. Remote datacenter calls include network round-trip times that can be hundreds of milliseconds, making them impractical for synchronous user-visible operations. A concrete example: if a user profile is frequently read, serving it from an in-memory cache gives sub-millisecond responses and reduces end-to-end latency significantly versus fetching from a remote SSD. A common misconception is assuming all persistent stores are equally suitable for reads; always match access patterns and latency requirements. Key takeaway: use memory for hot reads, SSD for warm data, disk for cold storage, and avoid cross-region syncs for latency-sensitive paths.

The second is being overly precise: avoid implying unwarranted precision — round to the nearest power of two or ten and justify it.
